overview: Zimbabwe’s regional history includes the workshops and farms of Great Zimbabwe, carved household objects and living musical traditions. These examples span different periods and communities; the modern republic is not the same political institution as the medieval capital.

periods.title: Southern Rhodesia under company administration
periods.summary: The map’s early Zimbabwe label refers to territory then called Southern Rhodesia. The British South Africa Company administered it before the 1923 transition to colonial self-government. This was not yet the independent Republic of Zimbabwe.

periods.title: Colonial self-government for a minority
periods.summary: Southern Rhodesia received self-government in 1923 under British sovereignty. White settlers dominated its government, while property and income requirements excluded the Black majority from political participation. Self-government in this setting did not mean equal political rights.

periods.title: A federation of three territories
periods.summary: Southern Rhodesia joined Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland in the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland in 1953. The federation ended in December 1963. Its three territories subsequently followed different political paths.

periods.title: After the federation
periods.summary: The federation had dissolved, but Southern Rhodesia had not become independent Zimbabwe. Northern Rhodesia became Zambia in October 1964, while the southern territory adopted the shorter name Rhodesia. Similar names can hide very different political histories.

periods.title: Unilateral declaration and liberation struggle
periods.summary: The white minority government declared independence in 1965. The United States did not recognise that declaration. Minority rule and the liberation struggle continued; Zimbabwe’s internationally recognised independence came in 1980.

periods.title: Lancaster House and the transition
periods.summary: The 1979 Lancaster House negotiations produced a new constitution, a ceasefire and the framework for elections. They formed part of the transition from war and minority rule to independent Zimbabwe.

periods.title: The independent republic
periods.summary: Zimbabwe became independent on 18 April 1980, when the United States recognised the republic and opened an embassy. This date marks the end of British sovereignty, not the beginning of the region’s communities and cultures.

periods.title: A new constitution
periods.summary: Zimbabwe adopted a new constitution in 2013, including provisions for women’s representation. This constitutional milestone occurred within the continuing republic.

periods.title: A change of president
periods.summary: Robert Mugabe resigned in 2017 after Parliament began impeachment proceedings. The change ended his presidency; it did not end Zimbabwe as a country.

periods.title: Musical knowledge across generations
periods.summary: In 2020, Malawi and Zimbabwe’s shared nomination for crafting and playing Mbira/Sansi joined UNESCO’s Representative List. Recognition concerned a living tradition, not a newly invented instrument.

sections.title: Small finds behind the famous walls

items.text: At Great Zimbabwe, archaeologists recovered ceramic discs used as weights when spinning cotton. These modest objects point to skilled textile work behind the much more conspicuous stone walls. A spindle weight is a clue to making thread, not a surviving wardrobe: it cannot tell us every garment people wore. The settlement’s occupation extended from about the eleventh into the seventeenth century.

Charred sorghum recovered at Great Zimbabwe provides evidence of a crop people used. Slag, ores and furnace tubes point to metalworking, while crucibles preserve another part of the craft process. These finds reveal farming and manufacturing alongside long-distance trade. A burned grain can help reconstruct a food history, although it cannot supply the cook’s complete recipe.

sections.title: A carefully carved place to rest

items.text: A wooden headrest by a Shona artist, dated from the late nineteenth to mid-twentieth century, has a small upper platform, a figure-eight-shaped base and a support carved with circles and angular patterns. The Met’s catalogue discusses several possible meanings for the decoration and leaves the question open. This household object shows considerable carving skill; we cannot read its owner’s dreams from the patterns.

Mbira/Sansi makers attach metal keys to a wooden board, sometimes adding a calabash or wooden resonator. UNESCO’s joint account for Malawi and Zimbabwe records keys made from spoon handles, bicycle spokes or spring wire. Fingers and thumbs pluck the keys. A piece of metal that once belonged in a kitchen or on a bicycle can take on a musical job.

Families have passed on mbira-making and playing through apprenticeship, while some schools and formal teachers also teach these skills. Musical patterns repeat with small changes and interwoven melodies. Learning involves hearing and practising those relationships, whether a relative teaches at home or an instructor leads a lesson.

Mbende Jerusarema is associated especially with Zezuru Shona communities in eastern Zimbabwe. UNESCO describes a master drummer, wooden clappers, handclapping, whistles and energetic movements by women and men. Some crouching and kicking movements imitate a burrowing mole. Coordinating all those parts is a group skill, even when a single master drummer leads the rhythm.

sections.title: A VIP with a very practical job

items.text: Peter Morgan dates his original Blair toilet design to 1973. Here VIP means ventilated improved pit: the design combines a pit with a vent pipe and a screen for flies. The pipe helps control smells, while the screen traps flies. The initials may sound glamorous, but the engineering tackles an everyday problem: making a toilet more pleasant to use.

Researchers studying 238 households with Blair VIP latrines in Mbire district during 2020 and 2021 found that some toilets lacked vent pipes or fly screens. Householders valued privacy and easy cleaning, but costs, flooding and incomplete construction could make facilities difficult to use. The study shows why inventing a useful toilet and keeping it working for a family are connected but different tasks.

sections.title: Classes before the campus was ready

items.text: The University of Zimbabwe’s history records early classes for about sixty-eight students at a temporary address on Baker Avenue, now Nelson Mandela Avenue. It dates these classes to 1952, before the 1955 royal charter and the move to Mount Pleasant in 1957. A university could begin with students and lessons while its permanent home was still taking shape.

The medical school opened in 1963 with an affiliation to the University of Birmingham. The institution later became the University of Rhodesia and was renamed the University of Zimbabwe after independence in 1980. Its history connects medical training with changing university partnerships and political institutions, without suggesting that every family had equal access to care.

The Smithsonian holds a Zimbabwean banknote with a face value of 100 trillion dollars: 100,000,000,000,000. It bears the date 2008 and pictures balancing rocks on one side, with Victoria Falls and a buffalo on the other. The enormous number belongs to a period of hyperinflation, when prices rose rapidly. More zeros on a note did not mean families could buy more with it.

sections.title: Family knowledge belongs in the kitchen too

items.text: In a 2019 FAO report from the Honde Valley, Loice Chideya invited her husband, Syndon Samukute, to a ten-day nutrition workshop. He then took up cooking for their children and demonstrated porridge made with ingredients including butternut squash and peanut butter. The story follows one family sharing skills and changing expectations about who prepares dinner.

The same programme organised nutrition circles where participants exchanged food-preparation knowledge and discussed hygiene and family care. Learning continued through conversation with neighbours as well as through workshops. The report describes a practical social gathering: people compared what to grow, what to cook and how to share household responsibilities.

ending.text: Zimbabwe’s independence on 18 April 1980 ended British sovereignty after the colonial period and the unrecognised Rhodesian declaration. The republic continues through later constitutional and political changes. The 1920 and 1960 map labels do not make it independent earlier, and the older Great Zimbabwe settlement belongs to a separate historical setting.
